## Problems (Total: 50 Points)

### Problem 1 (30)

A city's wastewater treatment plant discharges to an estuary where nitrogen feeds algal blooms that leave the water low in oxygen each summer. Its new permit requires it to remove at least 90 tonnes of nitrogen per year (t N/yr) more than it does now. The plant already converts the ammonia in its wastewater to nitrate. Its engineers have shortlisted four upgrades:

- **Anoxic zones** turn part of the aeration basins into unaerated zones, where bacteria convert nitrate to nitrogen gas (**denitrification**) using carbon already in the wastewater.
- A **methanol feed** adds methanol to the anoxic zones, giving those bacteria extra carbon so they remove more nitrate.
- **Sidestream treatment** is a separate reactor that treats the ammonia-rich liquid pressed out of the plant's digested sludge, before that liquid returns to the plant.
- A **denitrification filter** is a new filter at the end of the plant, where bacteria on the filter media remove nitrate from the effluent.

| Upgrade | Maximum removal (t N/yr) | Installation cost (\$1,000/yr) | Operating cost (\$/kg N removed) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Anoxic zones | 40 | 300 | 2 |
| Methanol feed | 40 | 20 | 5 |
| Sidestream treatment | 20 | 100 | 1 |
| Denitrification filter | 80 | 250 | 3 |

Installation costs are annualized: the construction cost is spread over the life of the upgrade, so the installation cost is per year, like the operating cost of a year's removal. An upgrade that is installed costs its full installation cost however much nitrogen it removes; one that is not installed costs nothing and removes nothing.

There are two rules governing which combinations of upgrades are allowed:

1. The sidestream reactor and the filter would both be built on the plant's one open site, which has room for only one of them (the **site rule**).
2. The methanol feeds the bacteria in the anoxic zones, so the methanol feed can be installed only if the anoxic zones are (the **methanol rule**).

The plant wants to meet its removal requirement at the lowest annual cost.

#### Problem 1.2 (10)

#### Problem 1.3 (6)

### Problem 2 (20)

A water utility must add ultraviolet (UV) disinfection to its drinking-water plant, as a second barrier against *Cryptosporidium*. It can buy two kinds of UV reactor:

| Reactor | Capacity (MGD) | Price (\$100,000) | Power (kW) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Medium-pressure | 5 | 2 | 10 |
| Low-pressure | 2 | 1 | 2 |

Medium-pressure reactors cost less per MGD of capacity, and low-pressure reactors use less power per MGD. A state grant covers \$1,000,000 of reactors, and the UV building's electrical service has 41 kW to spare. The utility wants as much UV capacity, in million gallons per day (MGD), as the grant and the power supply allow. With $x_1$ medium-pressure and $x_2$ low-pressure reactors, the problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max_{x_1, x_2} \quad & z = 5x_1 + 2x_2 && \text{(MGD)} \\
\text{subject to:} \quad & 2x_1 + x_2 \leq 10 && \text{(grant, \$100,000)} \\
& 10x_1 + 2x_2 \leq 41 && \text{(power, kW)} \\
& x_1, x_2 \geq 0, \ \text{integer}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Solve it by branch and bound, by hand.

#### Problem 2.1 (7)

Node 1 is the LP relaxation: the same problem without the integer requirement. Sketch its feasible region with $x_1$ on the horizontal axis, label each corner with its coordinates, and find node 1's LP optimum and its $z$. Is that $z$ an upper or a lower bound on the best capacity the utility can actually buy? Why?

#### Problem 2.2 (13)

Branch on $x_1$: node 2 adds $x_1 \leq 3$, and node 3 adds $x_1 \geq 4$. Solve the LP at each node (a sketch with its corners is enough), and report each solution and its $z$. Which node(s) can be pruned, and by which rule? What is the best purchase, and its capacity?
